textbookText: They are found on the vomer bone. Teeth in frog are not used for chewing purpose instead they are used to hold the prey inside the buccal cavity after the food is captured by tongue. The teeth are homodont i.e. similar shaped. They are curved backwards and directly attached to the jaw bones called acrodont condition. Old and worn out teeth are being continuously shed off during the life span and replaced by new ones and hence called polyphyodont. Each tooth is conical shaped consisting of mainly two parts: base and crown. The broad bony base is attached to the jaw bone. The crown is primarily composed of dentine and traversed by numerous fine branching canals called canaliculi. Tip of the crown is coated with a very hard and shining white substance called enamel (secreted by ameloblast cell). The internal cavity of tooth is called pulp cavity which is filled with a highly vascular and nutritive tissue, odontoblast cells (dentine secreting cells) and nerves. ii. Internal Nostrils:

The buccal cavity in its roof near vomerine teeth contains paired openings called internal or posterior nostrils which communicate with external nostrils. iii. Tongue: Tongue is large, thick, fleshy and protrusible structure lying on the floor of buccal cavity. It is attached anteriorly to the inner border of lower jaw; free and notched (bifid) posteriorly. Its upper surface bears taste buds in the form of small papillae. Secretion of tubular lingual glands and intermaxillary gland inside buccal cavity make the tongue adhesive. Such a sticky tongue can be thrown out and retracted suddenly by frog to capture live prey. iv. Bulgings of Orbits: The roof of buccal cavity just behind the vomerine teeth contains two large, soft, oval and cushion like areas the bulgings of orbits and eyeballs. While swallowing food, eyes are depressed, pushing the food backward.

v. Eustachean openings: Openings of Eustachian tube into the buccal cavity, each situated at the posterolateral side of roof of bucco-pharyngeal cavity. They communicate with the middle ear. vi. Vocal sacs opening: In male frog, there are two openings of vocal sacs, each present in the angle of two jaws on the floor of bucco-pharyngeal cavity. Vocal sacs amplify the sound at the time of croaking. vii. Glottis and gullet: Glottis is a median longitudinal slit like aperture in the posterior side of buccopharyngeal cavity, just behind the tongue. It opens while breathing so that air is passed to lungs and closes at the time of swallowing food. Similarly, Bucco-pharyngeal cavity posteriorly leads into the oesophagus through a transverse opening called gullet. viii. Fossae and prelingual elevations Fossae are three in number which are minute pits or depressions at the apical part of upper jaw, just below the maxillary teeth. Front end of lower jaw contains three small elevations, called prelingual elevations. Prelingual elevations fit into fossae to close the mouth tightly.

Buccopharyngeal cavity leads behind into a short, and stretchable muscular tube called oesophagus. Its inner lining is thrown into a large number of longitudinal folds for the sufficient distension of the oesophagus during the passage of the ingested food to the stomach. It abruptly leads into the stomach as there is no distinct demarcation between the oesophagus and stomach. Its inner wall also contains peptic glands and goblet cells.

4. Stomach: Stomach is a J-shaped muscular sac like structure situated in the left side of the body cavity or the coelom and attached to dorsal body wall by a mesentery called mesogaster. It is divided into two regions – the anterior large and wider region is called cardiac stomach and the posterior short narrower region is called pyloric stomach. The internal lining (mucous epithelium) of the stomach is thrown into numerous longitudinal folds which may allow the expansion of the stomach whenever required. Its mucous epithelium also possesses multicellular gastric glands which secrete pepsinogen enzyme, and unicellular oxyntic cells that secrete hydrochloric acid. Stomach also contains goblet cells which secrete mucus for lubricating food. The pyloric end of stomach is constricted externally and its opening into small intestine is internally guarded by a muscular ring or flap like sphincter or pyloric valve. This valve checks reverse flow of food from the intestine into the stomach. Function of stomach is to store food for few hours and also digest the food.
